text:
HSTU (2024) combines relative position/time attention bias, pointwise SiLU attention aggregation, and multiplicative gating. These mechanisms support learning time-sensitive dependencies, but its gate does not explicitly identify short-term intent or completed needs. Relative temporal bias provides a natural place to model elapsed-time effects while preserving the HSTU backbone. [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152).

Later research supports distinguishing persistent preferences from recent activity. “Don’t Waste It” (2025) introduces jointly trained, prior-conditioned adapter heads for interpretable dimensions including long- versus short-term interests. Rec2PM (2026) compresses histories into preference-memory tokens, reporting denoising and robust long-term-interest retention. HPGR (2026) explicitly models session structure and uses preference-guided sparse attention to select relevant history. These offer related design evidence, without establishing that recency alone identifies the user’s current task. [Temporal priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10492), [Rec2PM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11605), [HPGR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00980).

Experiment hypothesis: retain one jointly trained HSTU per category; add bucketed elapsed-time bias and a learned internal gate conditioned on recent hidden states and observed history gaps to regulate historical contributions. Train causally for next-item prediction; compare temporal bias alone against bias plus gating using fixed validation HR@10. Use only timestamps available at prediction, never the next interaction’s timestamp. Treat session boundaries, interest persistence, and fulfilled needs as inferred hypotheses; timestamps provide no direct labels for them. Any benefit on these Amazon categories remains unverified.
